question: What helped the campaign change bus rights?
status: These five cards are new teaching summaries. The lesson writer made them in 2026. No old text or picture is copied. The record or history behind each card has its own maker and purpose.

source_cards.title: A call to stay off buses
source_cards.maker: Women’s Political Council members and local leaders
source_cards.purpose: To get people to join a protest
source_cards.body: Jo Ann Robinson and other organisers helped spread a leaflet. It asked Black residents to avoid the buses on Monday 5 December. The first call was for one day. The protest then grew into a much longer boycott.
source_cards.question: Does a call to act prove that everyone joined?
source_cards.help: It is useful for what organisers asked people to do. It cannot count how many joined.
source_cards.staff: The King Institute catalogue marks the leaflet’s author and 2 December date as uncertain. Its note identifies WPC preparation and later editing by a committee of local leaders. Early December is used on the pupil card; do not attribute every version to one author. The extended boycott is context from H1, not a statement that the first leaflet planned a year.

source_cards.title: The early demands
source_cards.maker: MIA leaders, Martin Luther King Jr and U. J. Fields
source_cards.purpose: To ask the bus company to change its rules
source_cards.body: The MIA was the group that led the boycott. Its early demands included polite treatment, seats taken in order of arrival, and Black drivers on mainly Black routes. The seating plan still placed Black riders from the back and White riders from the front. These demands did not yet seek fully mixed seating.
source_cards.question: Does a list of demands prove they were met?
source_cards.help: It gives evidence of leaders’ aims at that time. It does not prove the company agreed.
source_cards.staff: MIA means Montgomery Improvement Association. The document catalogue gives an approximate 8 December date; the historical overview reports formal demands on 8 December. First-come seating was proposed within a front/rear arrangement, not a demand to retain reserved empty seats. Do not turn early limited demands into full integration from the outset.

source_cards.title: Keeping the protest going
source_cards.date: A later history, updated in 2022, about 1955–1956
source_cards.purpose: To explain how the boycott worked
source_cards.body: Many people walked or shared car rides so they could stay off buses. Volunteers drove and helped arrange lifts. The MIA raised money to support this work. The campaign needed many people and steady effort, not just one famous leader.
source_cards.question: Can a short history tell us about every journey?
source_cards.help: It helps explain how people travelled during the boycott. The broad account is checked against another history. It leaves out many daily details.
source_cards.staff: The NPS and King Institute accounts agree on carpools, volunteers and fundraising. They differ on some counts and the MIA founding date; those disputed details are not used. Later histories can combine records but must be checked, including institutional sources. Do not claim that every boycotter used the carpool.

source_cards.title: The court ruling
source_cards.kind: Court decisions described in a later history
source_cards.maker: Courts made the rulings; the King Institute wrote the later history
source_cards.purpose: To explain court decisions about bus segregation
source_cards.body: Four Black women challenged bus segregation in the case Browder v. Gayle. On 5 June, federal judges ruled against the segregation laws. On 13 November, the US Supreme Court upheld that ruling. The legal case mattered as well as the boycott.
source_cards.question: Does a court ruling tell us how every rider was treated?
source_cards.help: The account gives evidence of a change in law. A legal ruling cannot show every person’s daily experience.
source_cards.staff: This card summarises the King Institute’s account of the decisions, cross-checked with NPS; the original court opinion is not supplied. The district court majority was two to one. Four plaintiffs continued the case after a fifth original plaintiff withdrew. Rosa Parks was not a plaintiff in Browder v. Gayle. Name women and lawyers if helpful without suggesting that one leader secured the change alone.

source_cards.title: A call to end the boycott
source_cards.maker: Martin Luther King Jr for the MIA
source_cards.purpose: To announce the next step after the court order arrived
source_cards.body: The court order had reached Montgomery. King announced that the boycott was ending. He asked Black residents to return to buses the next morning with the seating rule removed. His call shows what the leaders wanted people to do next. It does not, by itself, show every bus journey.
source_cards.question: How could we check whether the plan happened?
source_cards.help: It is strong evidence of the public announcement. Check another account for what happened the next day.
source_cards.staff: The historical statement is paraphrased without any quotation. The King Institute’s editorial note and overview record integrated buses on 21 December 1956. This is a check beyond the statement’s call. Ending segregation on buses did not remove every discriminatory rule or end racism. No slurs, testimony or violence details are needed.

model.status: Original teaching model; no historical quotation or footage.
model.text: S1 tells me that organisers asked people to avoid buses on 5 December. The lesson writer made this card. A campaign group made the leaflet behind it to gain support. I trust it for the plan. It does not prove that every person took part. I would check an account of what happened.
